questions.stem:
Select the exact correct indirect form of the given direct sentence.

He said, "I am reading a book."

options.option_text: He clearly said that he is reading a book.
He said that he was reading a book.
He said that I was actually reading a book.
He said he has been reading a great book.

questions.explanation: The reporting verb 'said' is in the past tense, so the present continuous tense inside the quotes ('am reading') must change to the past continuous tense ('was reading'). The pronoun 'I' changes to 'he'.

questions.stem:
Select the exact correct indirect form of the given direct sentence.

She said to me, "I will call you tomorrow."

options.option_text: She told me that she will eagerly call me tomorrow.
She told me that I would definitely call her the next day.
She told me that she would call me the next day.
She said to me she would excitedly call me tomorrow.

questions.explanation: 'Said to' changes to 'told'. The pronoun 'I' changes to 'she', and 'you' changes to 'me'. The modal 'will' changes to its past equivalent 'would'. The time word 'tomorrow' must change to 'the next day' in indirect speech.

questions.stem:
Select the exact correct indirect form of the given direct interrogative sentence.

He said, "Has anyone seen my keys?"

options.option_text: He asked if anyone has seen his keys.
He asked that if anyone had seen his keys.
He asked whether anyone saw his keys.
He asked if anyone had seen his keys.

questions.explanation: For yes/no questions, the reporting verb changes to 'asked' and we use 'if' or 'whether' to connect. The present perfect tense ('has seen') changes to the past perfect tense ('had seen'). We do not use 'that' before 'if'.

questions.stem:
Select the exact correct indirect form of the given direct imperative sentence.

The teacher said to the boys, "Do not make a noise."

options.option_text: The teacher ordered the boys not to make a noise.
The teacher ordered the boys to not make a noise.
The teacher ordered the boys that do not make a noise.
The teacher strongly forbade the boys not to make a noise.

questions.explanation: In imperative sentences, 'said to' changes to 'ordered', 'requested', etc. The negative imperative 'Do not' changes to 'not to' before the infinitive verb. 'Forbade' implies a negative already, so 'forbade... not to' is grammatically incorrect due to the double negative.

questions.stem:
Select the exact correct indirect form of the given direct imperative sentence.

"Please bring me a glass of water," she said to him.

options.option_text: She ordered him to bring her a glass of water.
She requested him that bring me a glass of water.
She requested him to bring her a glass of water.
She told him to completely bring me a glass of water.

questions.explanation: The word 'Please' indicates a request, so the reporting verb 'said to' changes to 'requested'. The imperative verb 'bring' connects using the infinitive marker 'to'. The pronoun 'me' changes to 'her'.

questions.stem:
Select the exact correct indirect form of the given direct exclamatory sentence.

He said, "Alas! I am ruined."

options.option_text: He exclaimed with joy that he was ruined.
He exclaimed with sorrow that he was ruined.
He exclaimed with sorrow that I am ruined.
He exclaimed sadly that he is heavily ruined.

questions.explanation: The interjection 'Alas!' expresses sorrow, so the reporting verb changes to 'exclaimed with sorrow'. The conjunction 'that' is used, and the present tense 'am ruined' changes to the past tense 'was ruined'.

questions.stem:
Select the exact correct indirect form of the given direct exclamatory sentence.

The captain said, "Bravo! You have played well."

options.option_text: The captain applauded him, saying that you had played well.
The captain exclaimed with joy that he has played well.
The captain praised him, saying that he has played well.
The captain applauded him, saying that he had played well.

questions.explanation: The interjection 'Bravo!' indicates applause or praise. The standard transformation is 'applauded [object], saying that...'. The present perfect tense 'have played' must change to the past perfect tense 'had played'.

questions.stem: He said to her, 'I met your brother here yesterday.' Which of the following is the correct indirect form?

options.option_text: He told her that he had met her brother here the day before.
He told her that he met her brother there the previous day.
He told her that he had met her brother there the previous day.
He told her that he had met her brother there yesterday.

questions.explanation: C is correct because three simultaneous changes are required: (1) 'met' (simple past) backshifts to 'had met' (past perfect); (2) the place adverb 'here' changes to 'there'; (3) the time adverb 'yesterday' changes to 'the previous day'. Option A retains 'here' unchanged. Option B fails to backshift 'met' to 'had met'. Option D retains 'yesterday' instead of changing it to 'the previous day'.

questions.stem: The manager said to the employee, 'Why did you come late today?' Which option correctly converts this into indirect speech?

options.option_text: The manager asked the employee why did he come late today.
The manager asked the employee why he came late that day.
The manager asked the employee why he had come late that day.
The manager asked the employee why had he come late that day.

questions.explanation: C is correct: for WH-questions, 'asked' is the reporting verb; the WH-word acts as conjunction so no subject-verb inversion is used; 'did you come' backshifts to 'he had come' (past perfect); 'today' changes to 'that day'. Option A retains both inverted word order and 'today'. Option B correctly removes inversion but fails to shift simple past to past perfect — competitive exams require past perfect here. Option D retains the interrogative inversion after the WH-word.

questions.stem: Riya said to her friend, 'Your sister told me that she will visit us next week.' Identify the correct indirect form of this nested reported speech.

options.option_text: Riya told her friend that her sister told her she would visit them the following week.
Riya told her friend that her sister had told her she would visit them the following week.
Riya told her friend that her sister had told her she will visit them the following week.
Riya told her friend that her sister had told her she would visit us the following week.

questions.explanation: B is correct: in the embedded clause, 'told' (simple past) backshifts to 'had told'; 'will' changes to 'would'; 'Your' changes to 'her'; 'me' (Riya) changes to 'her'; 'us' (Riya + friend) changes to 'them'; 'next week' becomes 'the following week'. Option A fails to backshift 'told' to 'had told'. Option C retains 'will' unchanged. Option D retains the first-person 'us' instead of changing it to 'them', a classic pronoun error in nested structures.

questions.stem: The children said, 'Let us play football in the park.' Which of the following is the correct indirect form?

options.option_text: The children said that let them play football in the park.
The children suggested that they should play football in the park.
The children told that they would play football in the park.
The children requested that they should play football in the park.

questions.explanation: B is correct: 'Let us…' is a proposal/suggestion, so the reporting verb becomes 'suggested' or 'proposed', and the structure changes to 'that they should + base verb'. Option A wrongly retains 'let' in the indirect clause — 'said that let' is ungrammatical. Option C uses 'told that', which is incorrect for a suggestion, and 'would' misrepresents the mood. Option D uses 'requested', which implies asking an outside party for a favour; 'let us' is a mutual proposal, not a request directed at someone else.

questions.stem: The priest said to the devotees, 'May God grant you peace and prosperity!' What is the correct indirect form of this optative sentence?

options.option_text: The priest said that God may grant them peace and prosperity.
The priest prayed that God might grant them peace and prosperity.
The priest wished that God would grant them peace and prosperity.
The priest told the devotees that God might grant them peace and prosperity.

questions.explanation: B is correct: optative sentences ('May + subject + verb') are reported using 'prayed' or 'wished'; 'may' backshifts to 'might'; 'you' changes to 'them'. Option A uses 'said that' (wrong reporting verb for an optative) and keeps 'may' unchanged. Option C uses 'would' as the modal, but 'would' is not the backshift of optative 'may'; 'might' is the standard form. Option D uses 'told…that', which is the declarative pattern; optative sentences require 'prayed/wished that', not 'told that'.

questions.stem: She said to him, 'If I were the principal, I would change the examination pattern.' Which option correctly reports this sentence in indirect speech?

options.option_text: She told him that if she was the principal, she would change the examination pattern.
She told him that if she had been the principal, she would have changed the pattern.
She told him that if she were the principal, she would change the examination pattern.
She told him that if she were the principal, she would have changed the pattern.

questions.explanation: C is correct: in Type 2 (unreal present) conditionals, the subjunctive 'were' is preserved in indirect speech — it does NOT shift to 'was', and the result clause retains 'would + base verb'. Option A replaces the subjunctive 'were' with the indicative 'was', losing the hypothetical mood — the most common exam trap. Option B incorrectly converts the sentence to Type 3 structure ('had been…would have changed'), which reports a counterfactual about the past, not a present hypothesis. Option D mixes a Type 2 condition ('were') with a Type 3 result ('would have changed'), creating a structurally inconsistent conditional.

questions.stem: The student said, 'I wish I had studied harder before the examination.' Identify the correct indirect form.

options.option_text: The student said that he wishes he had studied harder before the examination.
The student said that he wished he had studied harder before the examination.
The student said that he wished he would have studied harder before the examination.
The student said that he wished he had been studying harder before the examination.

questions.explanation: B is correct: 'wish + past perfect' expresses regret about the past. In indirect speech, 'I wish I had studied' → 'he wished he had studied' — past perfect does NOT backshift further since it is already the furthest past form; only the pronoun and reporting verb change. Option A retains 'wishes' (present tense) instead of backshifting to 'wished'. Option C uses 'would have studied', which belongs in conditional result clauses, not in 'wish' constructions — a very common high-stakes error. Option D changes 'had studied' to 'had been studying' (past perfect continuous), altering the meaning from a completed action of preparation to an ongoing activity.
